newsitem.title: UK: IRA suspect names her baby "ray of sunshine".
newsitem.headline: IRA suspect names her baby "ray of sunshine".

text.p: IRA bomb suspect Roisin McAliskey, taken from prison to have her baby in a London hospital, on Tuesday named her daughter Loinnir, which in Irish means "sun shining through a dark cloud."

"I think that my grand-daughter has been named very appropriately and beautifully," said Irish civil rights campaigner Bernadette McAliskey, nee Devlin, who has been fighting for six months for her daughter's release.

The 25-year-old prisoner had been held in Britain's high security Holloway prison since last year pending extradition to Germany for questioning about an Irish Republican Army mortar attack at a British army base in Osnabrueck.
Depsite a difficult pregnancy and protest from the Dublin government and Roman Catholic politicians, Britain had consistently refused bail requests.

Bail was finally granted three days before the baby was born in a London hospital on Monday afternoon where the Republican firebrand Bernadette McAliskey praised the police for being "non-disruptive, minimal and non-intrusive."
She contrasted this sharply with the treatment she said her daughter had received in prison where she was even denied access to sanitary towels.
McAliskey said security officers even accompanied her to ante-natal classes in prison where the most intimate issues were being discussed.
"She was denied access to sanitary towels as a security risk. Her child's clothing was kept in a plastic bag outside her cell," McAliskey told reporters.
Roisin McAliskey is to remain in hospital until doctors say she is medically fit to be discharged. Lawyers would then seek unconditional bail for her pending the extradition proceedings.
Her mother said they have offered the court sureties from leading members of parliament as well as 100,000 pounds ($160,000) in cash and an agreed address where she would stay in London.

"There is no reasonable belief that Roisin McAliskey would abscond," she said. The only reason for her continued detention was the seriousness of the offence -- the attemped murder of 150 British soldiers.
McAliskey argued "There is not one single supportable shred of evidence to indicate that she has the most minimal knowledge of that offence".
She said the German evidence had now been reduced to one small piece of 'Sellophane' (adhesive tape) in a rubbish bag that they claim has her daughter's fingerprints on it.
"We are looking at a very strong case for bail again," said the former member of the British parliament.
